$comment: Committed §7.4 baseline for the VS Code smoke, compared against by test-e2e/run-smoke.mjs on every run. Raw samples are kept, not reduced away: a median whose numbers were discarded cannot be compared with the next one. Update deliberately, in a commit that says which runs replaced it and why.

recordedFrom.note: block 13 slice D; fifteen cold editor launches pooled across three sessions on one machine, with no product change between them

spread.$comment: Why this baseline is pooled, and what its comparison can and cannot detect. The first baseline was recorded from a single session of five launches (activation median 2948) and the very next run — with nothing changed in the product — reported +23.7% against it and raised a §7.4 alarm. Across three sessions activation ranges 2795–6493 ms and first open 1517–3640 ms: a 2.3x spread on the same machine, same commit, driven by whatever else the laptop was doing. The policy's 5% median threshold is therefore below this hardware's own noise floor, and a single-session comparison cannot separate a regression from a busy machine.
spread.consequence: The comparison stays in the receipt as an investigation trigger, exactly as §7.4 intends, and is deliberately not wired to fail the run. What a red comparison means here is 'look at the samples', not 'a regression happened'. A comparison that could actually decide needs either a quiet-machine protocol or many more launches, and neither belongs in a smoke run.
